title: The brothers bow (Genesis 42)
hook: his brothers come for grain and don't recognize him; he turns away and weeps

segments.voice: Yesterday, Pharaoh's dreams: seven fat cows, seven thin, and a prisoner who ended the day running Egypt. Your line: plan for the lean years.

The good years come, and Joseph fills the storehouses. Then the famine arrives, as the dreams said, all the way to Canaan, where old Jacob watches his family go hungry. He hears there's grain in Egypt: why do you just sit looking at one another? Go down and buy some. Ten brothers go. Benjamin, Rachel's other son, stays home. Jacob has already lost one of Rachel's boys; he won't risk the second. So ten men walk into Egypt to stand in line for bread, before the governor of the land.
screen: `THE FAMINE REACHES CANAAN.` → `TEN BROTHERS GO DOWN.` → `BENJAMIN STAYS HOME.`

segments.voice: In the King James Bible: "Joseph's brethren came, and bowed down themselves before him with their faces to the earth." The sheaves are bowing, and Joseph remembered the dreams, the text says. "Joseph knew his brethren, but they knew not him." Of course not. He was a teenager in a coat; now he's a grown Egyptian official, shaved, speaking through an interpreter. He speaks roughly, accuses them of being spies, and holds them three days. Then he lets them go, but keeps one brother, Simeon, bound, until they come back with the youngest. And the brothers, not knowing he understands every word, talk among themselves in their own language: "We are verily guilty concerning our brother, in that we saw the anguish of his soul, when he besought us, and we would not hear." All these years later, the pit is still in the room. Then: "And he turned himself about from them, and wept." The governor steps away so no one sees his face, cries, and comes back to keep testing them. Why test them? Genesis doesn't say. Readers wonder whether he wants to know if they've changed, or is simply hurt and doesn't know what to do yet. Genesis leaves both open. Look at the week behind us: Esau running to his brother, the coat, the pit, Potiphar's house, the forgotten prisoner, the dreams by the Nile. Under all of it sits a family that broke. And now the brothers say out loud what they did.
screen: `THE SHEAVES BOW AT LAST.` · `HE KNEW THEM; THEY KNEW NOT HIM.` · `WE ARE VERILY GUILTY.` · `THE GOVERNOR TURNS AWAY AND WEEPS.` · then, large: `AND HE TURNED HIMSELF ABOUT FROM THEM, AND WEPT.`

segments.voice: Maybe there was a time you turned away so no one would see you cry: at work, at a funeral, in the car before walking into the house. You don't have to cry now; just notice what was being carried then, and how long it was carried alone, and let your shoulders drop. If you pray, you can bring that moment to God; if you don't, be gentle with the person you were then.
Simeon. The brother Joseph holds back in Egypt, kept bound until the others return with their youngest brother.
Your line: he turned away and wept. They saw a governor; he saw his brothers. Until tomorrow.

howItsDone: Some Christians read Genesis 42 as a story about guilt surfacing years later, and preachers use the brothers' confession to talk about honesty and repentance within families.

fork.setup: you're Joseph. the brothers who sold you are bowing at your feet, and they don't know you. you understand every word they say to each other. what do you do?
options: tell them who you are at once.
speak roughly, test them, and turn away to weep.
have them all thrown in prison for good.
fork.reveal: he accuses them of spying, keeps Simeon, and sends them for Benjamin. and when he hears them admit their guilt, he turns away and weeps.

original.note: Hebrew: to weep. Joseph weeps again and again in the chapters that follow.

trapdoor: what you thought: Joseph gets his revenge on his brothers.
what it means: he tests them hard, but the scene turns on his tears, and the brothers' confession: we are verily guilty.
what a scholar hears: the brothers speak freely because Joseph uses an interpreter; the reader, like Joseph, hears what they think no one else understands.

chat.says: Why do Joseph's brothers suddenly feel guilty once they're in Egypt?
options: Accused as spies, they remembered the pit: we saw our brother's anguish, and would not hear.
Joseph told them who he was right away, and they felt ashamed standing before him.
Simeon had confessed to their father that they sold Joseph, so they all owned up.
chat.meaning: Not knowing Joseph understood, the brothers said: we are verily guilty concerning our brother. Joseph turned away and wept.

notes: 'Twenty years after the dream': Joseph was 17 (37:2), 30 before Pharaoh (41:46), plus seven years of plenty and some famine; roughly twenty years. Confirm the round number.
Week-end look-back (days 365–370) folded into the end of the teach.
'He accuses them of being spies' (42:9) and Simeon bound (42:24). Confirm.
Joseph's weeping recurs (43:30; 45:2, 14–15; 46:29; 50:1, 17); the original note says 'again and again' rather than giving a count.
